title: Streams and overlap
brief: Stream a 256 MiB pinned host tensor through the GPU in chunks, apply a kernel, and copy it back, with one stream, a stream per chunk, and a stream per stage joined by events. Measure how close the overlap gets to the max(copy, compute) bound.
hints: The first call compiles the Triton kernel, which takes a few seconds, and the tests warm it up before they time anything.
torch.empty(n, dtype=torch.float32, pin_memory=True) gives a pinned tensor. Check it with tensor.is_pinned(). A copy from a pageable tensor runs, gives the right answer, and doesn't overlap.

Pass non_blocking=True to every copy_ in the pipeline, and don't call .item(), .cpu(), print a tensor, or synchronize inside it. The tests check that your function returns to the host long before the GPU finishes.

The buffers were allocated on the current stream, so each side stream must call s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream()) before it touches them. When the work is queued, make the current stream wait for every side stream with cur.wait_stream(s), so the tests' end event lands after all of it.

For pipeline_staged, record an Event on the copy-in stream after each chunk's copy, make the kernel stream wait_event on it, record another event after the kernel, and make the copy-out stream wait on that. A missing wait shows up as NaNs in the output, because the tests fill the device and host outputs with NaN first.
With n_streams = 1 the chunks run in order, so you should see no speedup over one big copy. That's expected, and it's the point.
The time model for n equal chunks is the sum of the three per-chunk stage times plus (n - 1) times the largest one. For three 8.52 ms stages and 8 chunks that's 10.65 ms.
